utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take today's appearances, please. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Gramsci De Fazio and Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Stanisic's Defence team: Slobodan Cvijetic [Realtime translation read in error "Zecevic"] and Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Your Honours, it's Slobodan Cvijetic, for the record, rather than Slobodan Zecevic; I think it has been recorded wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Professor Pasalic. Before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to continue his examination-in-chief, I remind you you are still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Cvijetic [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasalic, Professor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, we will move now to the chapter beginning with paragraph 13 in your report, which you entitled "Demographic Characteristics of the Population of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Period Between 1918 and 1991." Professor, you are practically dealing here with the historical context of the ethnodemographic changes and the ethnic composition of the areas which are the subject of your report. My question is this: Why should the historical context be relevant for such a report as this and, of course, for the particular subject that we are dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be aware of the presence and be a good visionary for the future, you have to have really good knowledge of the past when you are studying any phenomenon or process. In this case, considering the complexity of the ethnodemographic processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and viewing them in a long historical period, the historical context is unavoidable when drafting a report such as this one. So it is necessary to understand phenomena over a longer time-period. I limited myself to the twentieth century only as it is characterised by dramatic social, historical, and other events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, just like elsewhere. We cannot understand everything that was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the last decade of the twentieth century unless we are well aware of the history of this region. Historical events had a mostly indirect impact on all the contemporary events, let me call them so, which occurred from the beginning of the 1990s up until practically this day. This is why I thought that in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, but I'm reminding you to slow down because what you say has to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In this context, I drafted a chapter which dealt with the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1918 and 1991. I recall that two wars occurred in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this period in which large numbers of people perished. I said yesterday that the total number was around one million people in the First and Second World Wars. They were direct or indirect victims in these wars. That had a great impact on the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was reflected in the events that took place during the wars between 1991 and 1995. On the basis of what is stated in this chapter, we can follow all the complex and relevant demographic, ethnodemographic, and other movements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that everything is properly founded on facts here, that the sources are very relevant, as I emphasised in the report. Better studies and sources of data are not available for this kind of study dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina in the pre-war period. And when I say pre-war, I have in mind the latest war that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I will say, frankly, that the works of Ms. Tabeau and also the work of the Research and Documentation Centre in Sarajevo do not include this approach which I firmly believe reduces the comprehensiveness and the details of their studies. I repeat once again: You have to know really well the past of a specific area in order to be aware of the present moment and in order to be able to project what might happen in future. And when I say this, I only have in mind demographic developments, just to be clear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beginning in paragraph 29, you present rather precise data on the victims of all peoples who used to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the Second World War; Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Jews, and others. I am just interested, what were the sources from which you took the data about victims from this time-period?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I properly cited the sources of information which I believe to be the most relevant. The authors who produced these reports know more about these issues than I do; this is why I took the data from them. As explained in footnotes 6 and 7, there is a series of ethnic composition of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina produced by the University of Belgrade, it's faculty of geography, before the war which broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The sources concerning the victims of the 1941 to 1945 war are mentioned briefly just so that we would have the context and understand the continued troubles of the population in this area throughout history. There is also a map produced by Strahinja Kurdulija which I mention in footnote 7. So once again this is information that I took over from prestigious publications, as I, indeed, say in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, as for the area of Posavina, since I will be dealing with it later on, and the area of Krajina, are these two characteristic in this sense when it comes to the number of victims as discussed in your previous chapter, and who were these victims?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If victims from the Second World War are what you imply, Krajina is a wide region in Bosnia-Herzegovina which sustained most losses in the war in terms of percentages. It had the greatest number of victims in the Second World War. Posavina too, but not so much because the ethnic composition of the population is different in Posavina than in Krajina. Krajina was predominantly populated by the Serbs, whereas Posavina is characteristic by a greater mixture of Serbs and Croats. The percentage of the Bosniak population is just symbolic in the Posavina area. But if you had that in mind, it is quite certain that this was reflected, I would say, in the war events between 1992 and 1995; namely, the population remembered or learned what happened during the previous wars, and everyone felt fear, insecurity, caution, and the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina which became a certainty at one moment instilled a dose of fear in the entire population. We mentioned that yesterday and we will prove it by official data about refugees, displaced persons, the victims of the war, cleansing, ethnic cleansing, deportation within Bosnia-Herzegovina and outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina and including, as I would emphasise, all the ethnic groups. There was no selection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, in section 3 which begins with paragraph 74, you deal with forced migrations of the Serbian population region by region. And under paragraph 79 you briefly state the reasons why you are dealing with Serbian migrations. Can you please answer in more detail and explain why forced migrations of the Serbian population should be relevant for this case and for your report.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start by saying this: It is noticeable that earlier studies, and I primarily have in mind the research and the report of Ms. Tabeau, dealt with other ethnic groups. I also have in mind the studies of other researchers who did not do such a detailed study of the area. During the war between 1992 and 1995, I conducted some research as a member of an institution, not as an individual or a private person, an institution which was called a State Documentation Centre for the Research of War Crimes Against the Members of the Serbian People. Had I even wished, I was unable to study forced migrations of other peoples because I was limited in my movements just like all the other inhabitants because the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the control of various military formations. For this reason, I continuously, for five full years, studied these processes, that is to say, migrations which are mostly forced in war, even though we may classify them, as I said yesterday, as ethnic cleansing, deportation, and population transfer. So I limited myself to the areas in which I studied the migrations or, to be even more specific, forced migrations, of the Serbian population within Bosnia and Herzegovina. In order to ensure that my work would be of highest possible quality and as comprehensive as possible, I conditionally divided the area which I studied into ten regions, considering the war time circumstances. I said conditionally because if I took a scientific view of the regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina then it would look somewhat different than as I presented in this report and in the context of the war. While analysing these regions, as they may be conditionally called, I obtained relevant data primarily, as I already pointed out, by empirical research, which is the highest level of scientific research in science, in terms of research. But this is not all. You will see in the attached annexes that I also used official sources of information, the ones which were the most relevant at the time, and these were population censuses. By combining these various approaches, we managed to obtain the best available information at the time. However, I wish to emphasise quite objectively that the numbers and the research results which I established should be considered final. I do not think that the whole process has been finalised and that we have reached final results. So far no one has managed to do that for the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including there the work done by Ms. Ewa Tabeau. She herself admitted that directly in a quotation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 79 you say that the movement of the Serbian population has an initial character. I'm going to use the same terminology that is used by you, demographers, and you say that it is a chain reaction that then initialises the movements of other ethnic groups. Did I quote you properly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the essence. As I have already pointed out, it is necessary to emphasise the complexity of all the processes and movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the whole population. And as we know, the population comprises of the three ethnic group, three constituent peoples, as well as members of other peoples. If we study all this in a comprehensive way, we obtain a realistic and a comprehensive picture of all the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina including the demographic aspect that we are discussing today. We could, of course, also touch upon other subjects, but that is not my task here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in chapter 3 that you entitle "Ethnodemographic Changes in BH During the War, 1992 to 1995," and in the subheading "Posavina" on the following page, you deal with one of the ten regions that you mention; is that so? Before I ask you a specific question, I want to ask you the following: Is that the area through which the municipalities linked to the so-called corridor -- and everybody here at this Tribunal knows about the corridor, so I simply want to ask you, is that the area that you are discussing here?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it briefly, yes. So that is the reason why the demographic movement during the war in this very complex area that we researched, and it will be very interesting to hear some of my findings that I'm ready to present to you now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I will not go into all ten regions because we can find the details in your report. I would like to pause here at this area which is very important for the Defence. In paragraph 81 and especially 82, you say that the war practically moved from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina crossing through this specific area. You say that this was the territory of the Bosanski Brod municipality where that large crime was committed involving 256 Bosnian Serb civilians. Did this movement of the war from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, did it initialise all the movements of the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did this initiative, so it be called, start in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is stated here in the report, and this is also the official position, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina began right here in this area. It happened in March 1992. That's when the first victims lost their lives. And we find here a precise number: 256 civilians were killed. And about 30.000 Serbs in Posavina set out from their homes and hearths and began moving to other areas. In paragraph 81, we find precise data, relative data, which outlines the percentages of Serbs living in individual municipalities in the area of Posavina. These are the results of the population census from 1991. Bearing in mind that the war practically began in this area, and also since we know that the regular Army of the Republic of Croatia entered this area and that's when the casualties occurred, the conflicts then started to move to other areas. At the time, Posavina was practically emptied of its Serb population. The Croat population was dominant there. And as I have already mentioned, there was a small percentage of Bosniaks. We are probably going to see during the rest of my testimony that this area changed hands on a number of occasions and that is also the reason for the movements of the population. Let us take, for example, the town of Modrica which is situated in Posavina. It changed its population on a number of occasions. The population withdrew, fleeing before the military formations looking for more secure areas for temporary occupation. This is characteristic of the whole of Posavina. And then, as we have already mentioned, the domino effect, or the chain reaction, spread the conflict to other areas within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It happened because a large transfer of population began from certain areas and then they went looking for more peaceful areas which had not been the place of the conflict before. If you look into the annexes, you will find specific data about the suffering of Serb population in the areas that I researched in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, of course Bosanski Brod was not the only target of Croatian Armed Forces. You know that at a certain point the corridor was broken into two because a number of municipalities were taken over. What I would like to know is the following: Did the same process occur in those municipalities as well? And I'm talking here about the movement of population.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. You can find it here. We are not talking only about Bosanski Brod. It all began in Bosanski Brod when regular Croatian Armed Forces crossed the Sava River and enter Bosanski Brod. After that, the situation spread to Derventa, that is the following border municipality, with a relatively large number of Serbs living in it. After that, the process spread towards Modrica and partly towards Doboj because -- MR. Di FAZIO: Your Honour, please, I'm having great trouble following all of this evidence, and I'm not sure if the witness is perhaps straying into matters that are far beyond his expertise, namely military history, but he keeps talking about that the processes going on and occurring and flowing on from certain events, and I have no idea, frankly, what he's talking about, and I fear that the Chamber might not have any idea. We should be clear if the witness is talking about migration movements or population movements or demographic movements or whether he's talking about military events. I can't distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless I misunderstood the earlier remarks of the witness, his conclusions are that the population movements are interwoven with these military events. And as he is recounting the -- what happened at this point, I don't know that it is impermissible for him to attempt to separate out the military events which, as I understand his testimony, as I said, I may be completely misled or misunderstand what he is saying, is the context in which all of this is happening. MR. Di FAZIO: Very well, Your Honours. But I would alert you to -- or I do have misgivings about the fact that he may be straying into, firstly, areas of military history; and, secondly, when he does provide his evidence, it's not clear to me if he's talking about migrational movements or military consequences of certain actions. For example, when he talks about the regular Croatian Armed Forces crossing the Sava and entering Bosanski Brod, after the that the situation spread to Derventa and that is the following border and then the process spread towards Modrica; what did? The military processes or the migrational movements? How do we know all of this? It's not clear from the testimony, and that's my -- the cause of my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, it may be helpful for you to guide -- you take Mr. Di Fazio's point? It may be helpful to you to guide the witness in terms of separating the one from the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that your reasoning is very precise. You have understood the reasons because of which we are doing this. This expert is not talking about the military operations as a military expert. He is simply giving the context of the migrational movements of the population in the relevant areas. He simply touched upon the military operations as the direct cause of the movements. I will accept your suggestion and I'm immediately going to ask a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take, for instance, Modrica. You said that it is characteristic because it was under the control of various military forces on a number of occasions. Was it also accompanied by the movements of the population depending on under whose control the town was? We are talking, of course, about all the three populations.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, but I would like to respond to the intervention by the Prosecutor, if you would permit me, because it is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, it would be simpler if you were to be guided by counsel and answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All right. But in this case, I would like to emphasise the following: I'm trying to explain that everything that happened in the area of Posavina happened in a certain causal relationship. If you have consequences, then there should have been a cause. So if we are talking about migrations, we have to notice that the cause of those migrations were the interventions on part of military formations. It is certainly not my intention, and I have managed to avoid it in the whole of my report, to discuss military operations. I'm not qualified to do that. However, when you research a certain event, you have to discover its causes and explain its consequences. Transfer of the population, the deportation of the population, from this area and other areas, it is all simply a consequence of something, and that is the context that I tried to give while answering the specific question of the Defence. Let us take Modrica. The population of Modrica changed on a number of occasions. It all depended on other processes that were taking place in this area. During a certain period of time, Modrica was inhabited by Serbian population; after that by Muslim and Croat population; and then after certain events, the Serbian population returned to that area. Of course today this picture is different and all three ethnic groups live there, including all those who wanted to return to their previous homes. They were able to do that. So this is the context within which I'm viewing all the events, and that also includes your specific question relating to Modrica. Modrica is merely a representative example of all the events that occurred in the area of Posavina, from Bosanski Brod all the way to the area of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, do you have data about the direction of the movement of the population from the areas caught up in the war? Where did they seek shelter?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that period, and I'm talking about the beginning of the war, the population moved in that direction where it could move. By that I mean where it was possible to use the roads. Some of them went towards the area of Semberija; that is Bijeljina. Others went to the area of Ozren; that's the hinterland of the town of Doboj. Some of them stayed in the area of Doboj, while a contingent went towards -- west towards Krajina in the area of Banja Luka. So the displacement took place in all four directions, looking at the compass. And also, of course, towards the areas outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as much as circumstances permitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, now let us leave the introduction and go back to your thesis about the causes of demographic and ethnic movements in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You already told us there are sociological, political, economic, and other causes. I did not manage to pigeon-hole the movements in Posavina, to link them with one specific reason or cause. How would you do it? How would you categorise it? Please, use very simple language.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a better look at the factors that I enumerated in the introduction, then you will see that the dominant factor was the first factor, the political factor. I have already explained that it includes breaches of human rights, and we can see that at that moment there were serious human rights violations, peoples lives were threatened, they did not feel secure, so that is definitely a political factor. At the moment there was a certain risk for a certain ethnic group. In this particular case, we are talking about the Serbs who were threatened by other ethnic groups. This is very simple. These are facts. Of course, the main factor is always accompanied by the secondary factors, such as economic; the population was blockaded economically speaking. They did not have supplies of food, and there were no jobs. So that was another fear that set them into movement. Then there are the psychological factors, some of them objective, some of them more subjective. People wanted to link up with their families and also move the area because of some objective reasons. But I would like to emphasise that this is still the political factor. That was the dominant factor because there was still a risk posed by the other ethnic group that lived in the same area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we add something to that: That this is simply fleeing from the war and due to fear of war? I did not use a single demographic term at that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I explained that yesterday. War as a phenomenon creates fear, uncertainty among the population, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a wave of refugees due to that psychological factor. Not only due to coercion. Of course, that happened in this area as well. When the first victims fell, this created even greater uncertainty and led to even more fear among many people. Let me just point out that this was not the case only with one ethnic group. The members of all the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina were fleeing from the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the reasons I mentioned just now. They went elsewhere. Yesterday I refer to 2 million people that were on the move. That is practically half of the BH population according to the census. Out of a population of 4.370.000, 2 million were on the move. Not all of them were forced out, I mean by military forces. They simply pre-empted the situation in order to find a safer place to live because of the war that had engulfed the area. That is the essence on the basis of which you can understand what was happening in this area over the three or four years of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to clarify the last answer that you have just given. When you say that "2 million people were on the move," and then you add that "not all of them were forced out ... by military forces," but rather because of their attempt to pre-empt "the situation in order to find a safer place to live because of the war that had engulfed the area," this sounds to me to be a bit contradictory and I'm asking for a clarification, because if you say that they didn't move away from the place that they were living because of the war, then how come that you, in the next sentence, say that the reason they left was because of the war? I mean, you touched upon it yesterday as well, and you did maintain that at least some parts of the movements that took place in the area were really, and I think you used the word voluntary movements. And I had difficulty in understanding this correctly because my assumption would be, and you may contradict me if I have misunderstood this, my assumption would be that people don't just give up their houses and their farms and their places of residence without there being a very specific reason for doing so. And in war time, restrictions of movements are quite often limited. So to the extent in which people actually do move away from their residence in war time, my assumption would be that the majority of people who move do so because of the war. So maybe it is not a direct consequence of the war, but it is certainly an indirect consequence. In neither of these two cases, however, I would characterise the move as being voluntary. So could you clarify what you meant yesterday by "voluntary movement," and could you hold it up against your assumption just now that it was really the war who prompted most of the movements here, please? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The last thing I said came out in a sort of clumsy sentence. This was a war-engulfed area. I mean, they were actually pre-empting the situation; they were leaving areas that had not been engulfed by the war yet but that was about to be engulfed by the war. Yesterday I talked about voluntary migration, I think I pointed out under quotations marks. Technically that is not the way it is put in the paper, truth to tell, because we have to admit that in a war psychosis there is no voluntariness. The circumstances of war are such or if there is any kind of intimation that certain areas will be engulfed by war, leads to fear, insecurity, fear for one's own life, and then that started, under quotations marks, "voluntary migrations." I can illustrate that by concrete examples, families. I and my family left the town where we lived due to that psychosis, although no one expelled us. I felt this insecurity on the eve of a war, and that happened a few days before the armed conflict there. Your movements are restricted, you have to wait for bread in line for several hours, one bread per family per day, you are not free to communicate, all your movements and conversations are monitored. Although, let me say this as well, in that particular milieux, I was a rather prominent person, professionally speaking and politically speaking, if that is relevant, I was the last president of the Socialist Alliance of the Working People in my municipality. It was a broad movement encompassing all ethnic groups. However, at that time this was no longer important; it was only ethnicity that was considered to be important. That's how I spoke about these "voluntary migrations," although technically that is not referred to in my report in that way. I agree that war as an armed phenomenon cannot lead to sincere voluntariness. There is this psychosis of coercion involved in all cases but there is an indirect and direct effect in all areas. On my own example, I showed that this happened in an indirect way. It's not that anyone pointed a weapon at me directly and expelled me in that way. Yesterday I also explained that transfer of the population and deportation is not ethnic cleansing. Ethnic cleansing of the population is carried out only in areas where it is done quickly and by force. Throughout history, that happened in different international contexts and it also happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I'm trying to confirm and say in this way is that Ms. Tabeau's report and others did not categorise these migrations, and I think that it was indispensable to do that, to see what is ethnic cleansing, that is to say, removing the population, the undesirable population, from a particular area quickly and by force. On the other hand, what is transfer of population, and yet a more extreme version, that is, genocide. That is the fourth category, the fourth group that I'm referring to within the entire migrations of a population from an area due to armed conflict. What I wish to indicate in my paper was that this was not done in Ms. Tabeau's paper or in some other papers and that would have been indispensable. However, I just indicated the problem. I did not elaborate on it either to such an extent. Quite simply, I did not have the proper capacities from -- for that from the point of view of knowledge and so on. I hope that this is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think I have understood you correctly. But are you suggesting that when people move in a time when the area in which they live is engulfed in armed conflict then there are basically two reasons: One part of the people who move away do so because they are targeted, and in that case you call it ethnic cleansing; another part of the people move out of the area not because they are targeted, but because of the inconvenience caused by the armed conflict, insecurity, fear, and maybe other psychological reasons, but for those you call them voluntary movements? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. That is the essence, basically. However, then we have to carry out another categorisation in view of the population, and that is another one of shortcomings of Ms. Tabeau's paper and others. Namely, at the beginning of the war we know what the overall population is, and it is categorised into military persons and civilian persons. What you are referring to, that is to say, leaving due to the war, was primarily something that happened to civilians who were not directly targeted by the war. It was members of military units that were directly targeted by war. In that context, I was trying to prove here that there were mass transfers of the population or deportations out of fear and a feeling of a fear for one's life and a general feeling of insecurity, or if there had already been some armed conflicts. Therefore, it is indispensable in all of our papers to carry out yet another categorisation, soldiers, civilians. Later on I can explain what is one and what is the other. And I can explain what it looked like in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also what the shortcomings are of all of our papers, because we omitted to carry out such an important categorisation in view of civilian and military victims because to a large extent this creates a different picture if things are not this way, if we look at the suffering of civilians and members of the military belonging to a particular ethnic group. If I understand your question correctly, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't really making a distinction between civilian and military persons because my assumption was that if you belong to the targeted group and an attack is coming, then you would try to escape by moving away and you would do so regardless of whether you were a military person or a civilian person. So what you are introducing now is another subdistinction in which you suggest that if you belong to the targeted group and you are indeed a military person, then you might consider to stay on in order to defend the area; whereas those who fled away would then typically be persons who were not military, that is to say, civilians would seek to fly away from the area -- to flee away from the area in order to seek protection, while the military personnel would stay behind and defend the area. Does that provide a meaningful understanding of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The military will stay behind to defend the area if they can. They're protecting civilians who are leaving before them. However, if a certain territory falls, as they say in military speak, there is a selection among the undesirable population. In most cases, it is children, women, and the elderly that are deported. That is a military rule. And in most cases that is what happened in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I categorise as population transfer, not ethnic cleansing, although this was caused by the military conflicts between the two sides involved in any particular part in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what led to this mass transfer or, under quotation marks, "voluntary migrations" due to the danger looming over a particular territory because of an armed conflict. That is how I viewed the problem, and I think that basically that is what it is. However, unfortunately sometimes no selection was carried out and a great many civilians were the victims. They were victimised either by military or paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we are getting close to the core of the matter. Because I would have thought that if the purpose of the military operation was to drive away people who belonged to the targeted group, then once the area had fallen as a result of the attack, then the deportation of women and children and elderly would, in my view, be the perfect example of ethnic cleansing; but do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree. If we start from the qualification that ethnic cleansing is only what is carried out quickly and by force, in those situations, yes. However, since deportation was underway, deportation of the population from a particular area, we cannot consider that to be ethnic cleansing. That is, indeed, removal of an undesirable population, but it was not carried out quickly and by force. There were some intentions of planned removals, then we have to touch upon the nature of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is what I do not like to deal with in my paper because that is not my field. Partly it was a civil war, partly it was a religious war, and in part it was a fight for certain territories. That is why the presence of a particular ethnic group was undesirable in a particular area. However, we cannot consider all of it to be ethnic cleansing. That is where I disagree. I repeat: I proceed from my understanding of ethnic cleansing and that is something that is carried out quickly and by force. I gave you my very own example, and I'm one of the many thousands of persons who left certain areas for various reasons, although this was not done quickly or by force in my case or in the case of other individuals in a particular area. That is how I explained that process, bearing in mind this qualification of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Back to you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I wonder, Professor, whether we have a linguistic or translation problem here. When you talk about deportation, what do you mean by that word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Deportation means expulsion of population in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia. It's expulsion but not by force. And when I say by force, I mean it is done quickly, say, in five hours, for example. You can take just the bare essentials, the minimum amount of money, and you have to leave a certain territory. I think that this is not a characteristic of all events in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this is why we cannot include it all in ethnic cleansing. This is why we talk about this term deportation which has been internationally established and also transfer of population which is a less severe variation of expulsion in war-time circumstances. We can illustrate this with numerous examples from the world. Nothing happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not already well-known practice internationally

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, Professor, in your view deportation has nothing to do with forcible transfer of or moving people, forcible? You say it has nothing to do with forced removal of population? So, for instance, your personal initiative to move out of fear, you qualify that as deportation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We have not understood each other. I said clearly that in armed forces any movement of the population comes under forced migration in a wider sense, but then we can make a classification of sub-categories: There are two extreme ones, genocide and ethnic cleansing; and two not so severe ones, one is deportation or expulsion and transfer of population. Under any war-time circumstances, there is nothing quite objectively voluntary. Maybe if someone was a good visionary, then half a year before the armed conflict he might have peacefully left a certain area. But in this case I'm talking about population movements by classifying them in these four categories. Perhaps some other subdivisions could have been made, and then it would have been even more precisely defined as part of a deportation or transfer and so on. However, none of that is voluntary. It is more or less forced, to a smaller or greater extent. Everything is to an extent forced directly or indirectly and it is taking place in areas which are affected by war. Any war, not just the one in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you briefly define the four categories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. Due to armed conflict or other conflicts, there are forced migrations of population. Let us leave aside the area. It doesn't matter if it's Bosnia-Herzegovina or some other place. Due to the forced migration, there are two extreme categories. They are genocide and ethnic cleansing, though we are not dealing with genocide here. Ethnic cleansing is only what is carried out fast and by force in a certain area, as I explained earlier. Between these two extreme categories, two less severe categories are deportation or expulsion and transfer or exchange of population. As, for example, in Cyprus between Turkey and Greece there was a transfer of population between the Northern and Southern Cypress, to be leave aside the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Or a deportation of the so-called undesirable ethnic group; well-known examples can be found internationally. I tried to explain this in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The essence of my efforts was to prove that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina what is often described in these cases as ethnic cleansing is not always that. There are less severe variants. So if I understood your question properly, this would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So what you did personally and what you call, under quotation marks, "voluntary movements," they are not within those three or four categories? They -- or not in the two last ones; they are not within deportation or transfer? Do I understand you right, correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it could be categorised as transfer because I left for an ethnic area populated by Serbs, and other ethnic groups left this area and moved into the area where I had been living. So if we take this example, we can talk about mass movements of population in Bosnia-Herzegovina which I described yesterday as ethnic homogenisation of the population. This is something that is well-known from other international practices. It was a sort of transfer, but we should not view it from an individual point of view, because a transfer is made up of a large group of people. I was not the only one who left in such a manner; it was just for the sake of illustration that I mentioned my example. But many other people left as well. And moving in the other direction were others who moved into the area which we left as the ethnic minority in that specific town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, the category of deportation is always imposed upon; the people deported, the people displaced, is forced; while transfer can be forced or "voluntary"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly so, but as compared to ethnic cleansing, deportation and expulsion take place over a longer period of time. You can prepare, this is announced, and then a certain group of people are transported to other areas. That also happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The good side of it with all this force, if I can put it so, is that the population was saved, and all these people from all ethnic groups are thankful that their lives were saved in the war and conflict. And transfer can be a matter of individual estimate or assessment, that it's good for you to remove yourself from a certain area at a certain moment, or it can be the so-called agreed transfer where one group of people moves to some other territory because yet another group of people who are members of another ethnic group would come to this specific area. All in all, these are very complex issues which have not been clarified sufficiently. We are just beginning to enter these issues. This is why I say that, with all due respect to the efforts made by Ms. Tabeau, some of these issues have not been sufficiently dealt with or analysed. It is so with all the rest of us and that is the point of what I'm saying. Much we are dealing with phenomena that have not been researched sufficiently, then we cannot draw proper conclusions because the research carried out has not been sufficient. This is what I keep coming back to and what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I have another five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite sufficient to agree with the dilemmas of the Trial Chamber, because I experienced them myself, and it's good that we heard this because some of my questions would have concerned what the Trial Chamber asked you. Tying up to the questions asked by Judge Delvoie, I will try to ask you something more simple. The transfer that you talked about in your last answer, could one say that the war imposed on people a situation in which people would choose the lesser of two evils? It is always bad, as Judge Harhoff said, when you have to leave your area. No one was glad to leave their home. But if greater evil lies in store for you if you stay, then, under quotation marks, as you say, voluntarily, you would assess that it's better for you to go away, to stay alive, and perhaps come back some day. So would my formulation that it is the choice of lesser of two evils something that is close to your definition of transfer?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite clearly, life is the greatest value that a man has. And that was the priority. And then the second thing would be thinking about your property, leaving your residence, whether the property would remain there and be saved or not. So the priority was to save the people's lives in the transfer because that's the greatest value that any individual has. I think that is quite clear and that it makes clear why there were mass transfers and other forms of migratory movements. So let me repeat for the third time, life was the priority for any inhabitant in war time and during the conflict and everything else that was taking place. So that was the core which caused mass transfers. Unfortunately, there were more severe forms in place as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the time. I think we are close to the time when we usually take the break. Perhaps it would be a good idea to have some rest now, break for a while, and then continue after the break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have been discussing a chapter in your report and I would like to finish this discussion. I think that the example of Posavina was a very good example for the relevant issues. I'm not going to go into any detail about the remaining nine regions, but I would like to ask a question that pertains to all nine regions. Was the same scenario played out in the nine remains regions in a similar way and is it possible to apply everything that you said about Posavina to the remaining nine regions?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Globally speaking, yes. But you have to take into account the specific circumstances of those individual regions. I'm talking about the number of aspects and especially about the demographic characteristics of the regions. There are some differences in ethnic composition in the population, in the age distribution of the population, their lifestyle, and other factors. But in essence, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you think that you have a characteristic example for some of the other regions, why don't you choose it yourself and comment it yourself? It was not my intention to go into any detail about the remaining regions. So only if you have some details that are different or particular interesting, I would invite you to present them to us.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, all these cases are interesting in their own way. I would like to emphasise briefly another area and that is Central Bosnia. Paragraph 85, 86, 87, including, of course, the annexes. Yesterday I already emphasised that this area contains the Bosniak population as the dominant population, and this is a typical example, where a process of ethnic and territorial homogenisation followed forced migrations. I have enumerated all the relevant municipalities here in the report. Serbian population left that area for some other areas where they felt more safe. In the report I gave very precise indicators. The largest town and municipality in that area was Zenica; absolutely speaking, the largest number of Serbs lived there. And if I may conclude, and it is my understanding that I'm permitted to say so, although this is not written in the report, today in the area of Central Bosnia we will find only a symbolic presence of a Serb population in all the municipalities. I hail from Zavidovici and I'm most familiar with the situation there, and I can say that in Zavidovici there is only one and a half thousand Serbs out of 11 and a half thousand Serbs who lived there according to data collected at the last population census in 1991. Similar processes took place in all ten regions that I mentioned. In areas where Serbs were minority or where they lived as a majority in a settlement that did not have status of municipality, in all such areas they had to leave their homes. You can find all this data in my tables in the annexes. You will find data and symbols that I used for all the settlements, all municipalities, and all local communes, as well as for each of the regions as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the last issue from that part. Everything that you present as a description in your report you also present as a table in Annex A, under the sub-annexes A1, -2, -3, and so on. For the reference in Serbian, Annex A begins at page 84. And in English version it begins at page 86. Can you turn to the first page that relates to Posavina, because we have spent most time on Posavina. And maybe you could use this example to explain your table, because I suppose that the same goes for all other tables. That will enable the Trial Chamber to understand the data contained in the tables. And then later on I will ask you something else. Did you find it in hard copy? You can also see it on the screen. You can choose whatever is more convenient for you. Maybe if we zoom in on the screen you will have a better view.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all the same. My eyesight is still very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I see that you are not wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I will now explain the methodology of my research. I have already spoken about it in my previous testimony. This is a combination of official statistical data. In the first column, you can find the results of the 1991 census. Or maybe, excuse me, I should be more clear. First we have the number for each municipality. After that we have the name of the municipality. For instance, Brcko, you can find this municipality here, and municipalities are always in bold. Then you can see total population according to the census from 1991. So these are official data. After that, from 1 to 6 you can see the names of the settlements within the Brcko municipality, the settlements in which certain population-related processes took place. Then you can see the column for the total population in 1991. You will find in this column the total number of inhabitants for each of the settlements. The following column gives the total number of Serbs. However, only there where Serbs comprised more than 50 per cent of the total population; that's why you will find the symbol for more than 50 per cent at the heading of this column. The next column shows the total number of Serbs in those settlements where they were minority, that is, in those settlements where there was less than 50 per cent Serbs. So this gives us an insight into the number of population -- number of settlements from which Serbian population was removed, where there were majority. And the same also for the settlements where they were minority. I would like to repeat once again that this data was taken over from the statistical bulletin, that is, the official publication that was published in the former Yugoslavia after the 1991 census by the federal statistical institute which collated all the data from all the republics. After that, we see the following columns: Settlements destroyed or burned. This column contains the results of my empirical research in the field from 1992 to 1996. These data are represented by symbols. If you see a symbol representing a house, it means that this settlement had been burned or devastated or destroyed in some other way, that is, the houses had been burned and looted. The next column is settlements from which Serbs had been -- MR. Di FAZIO: Your Honours, please, just perhaps if I may assist you. In the English you'll see a blank space; you won't see any house or any symbol. If you look at the B/C/S, that's where you see these little houses and tractors. I think tractors is meant to show expulsion and houses are destroyed settlements. So if it's blank in the English, it's a positive hit, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. I confess, I was struggling with the English version trying to understand the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously if you combine the two tables you will be able to follow the testimony. The English version does not contain the symbols; that is why you have to use both tables in order to find the actual contents. The Professor is obviously commenting the Serbian version and the symbols found in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I haven't even noticed that you don't have this in the English version, which makes it more difficult for you to use the tables. But you can, of course, always take a look at the Serbian version. We are not talking about numbers here, we are talking about symbols. So let me repeat. We have symbols for settlements which had been destroyed, and then you have a motor vehicle symbolising settlements from which the population left. The last column talks about execution sites of Serb population and the symbol is a cross. Such a symbol denotes an execution site where at least five persons lost their lives. And after that we arrived at the total numbers for each municipality and for each region. This region we call Posavina as a whole. You can find that at the end of this annex where it says "Posavina, total population according to census," and let me repeat it, I don't want any confusion to arise here: We are not talking about the total number of inhabitants of municipalities; we are talking here only about settlements and municipalities where those processes took place. And also I'm again specifying that I'm talking only about the places from which Serbs were expelled or killed. These are the results of the five-year research in the field that was conducted using standardised instruments. The state centre used standardised forms that were filled in in the field during the direct research, either through interviews, polls, or by personal insight. They are usual and acceptable methods of scientific research in those cases where other better, more relevant data are unavailable or where better ways of collecting data are unavailable. However, the research was conducted during the war, and this was a typical field research. I personally consider this the most valuable part of the report because these data cannot be found in any other statistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. I'm not going to go through all the other tables, they pertain to the other areas that you described. I'm going to move on to the next chapter in your paper. That is chapter number 4. It starts with paragraph 142 and you called it "Expelled Persons, Refugees, Displaced Persons, Households, and Holding Centres in Republika Srpska." Professor, the basic question is: What is the source of the information you refer to in this chapter? What was the source?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mention this and I formulate the heading in this way because I took this from official sources. My basic source which is referred to several times is the Census of Refugees and Displaced Persons in Republika Srpska in 1996. It was the Ministry for Refugees and Displaced Persons that was in charge of the process, and it says here "Sarajevo 1996." Perhaps someone doesn't understand why it says Sarajevo. It is due to the fact that the constitution of Republika Srpska says to this day that the capital is Sarajevo. So that is the basic source of information and we call it the primary source of information. Also secondary sources were used, namely books by certain authors. That is what I refer to in my footnotes, and you can see that. The most comprehensive book in relation to this chapter is, Spiric, Marijanac, "The Population of Republika Srpska," which was published by the faculty of economy in Banja Luka in 1999. I refer to these explanations specifically, along with each and every table, and I refer to the actual pages used, and of course I copied that from these textbooks so that I can perhaps use that here as well. This is officially-published data, and I accept them as such in number 4 within this chapter. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours, please, I thought the witness said that he got the information from a book that was written, then later he said it comes from officially-published data. I suggest that it's a relevant inquiry to find out where it comes from, a book or officially-published data.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we did not understand each other properly, let me say that the information comes from the primary source, namely the Census of Refugees and Displaced Persons in Republika Srpska in 1996. The book uses those data only. I took them over from the book and I make a correct reference to that in the footnotes. Underneath the tables I refer to the primary source, and in the footnote I say where I took the data from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, at any rate, the source, the primary source, is the census?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book was a secondary source for me, a book that referred to the data from there. The most important thing is that the data is primary data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Professor, paragraph 144. We go back to the figure of 2 million persons who were moved, as you had put it, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this pertains to all three main ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now here you have the actual data involved, how many Serbs, Croats, Muslims were moved from their places of residence; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information comes from the census; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, there is a particular piece of information that confused me and I believe that we should therefore try to clarify it now. If we move on to your next chapter, this starts with paragraph 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have paragraph 165 on our screens now. Could we also zoom in on that paragraph. Let's just wait for the Serbian version as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, this confused me, and I therefore think that you should explain this. In paragraph 144 you talk about 2 million people from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were moved, and then in paragraph 165 you refer to the same figure, 2 million persons fled or were expelled and displaced from the former Yugoslav republics, all of them, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Macedonia. From a linguistic point of view, one when reads this one gets the impression that the same figure is used for two different areas. Or perhaps the mistake is mine. Could you please explain what the 2 million Bosnia-Herzegovina pertains to and what this other 2 million pertains to from all the republics of the former Yugoslavia? Could you please start from paragraph 144 and tell us what that means directly, that 2 million.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the impression that one gains. Since I took these data over, I interpret them in the following way: In paragraph 144, there's a reference to 2 million people within Bosnia-Herzegovina who belong to this category of expelled persons, refugees, and displaced persons. That is not in dispute. Explicit figures are provided here for all three ethnic groups. My interpretation of paragraph 165 is that in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, within that area, about 2 million people were on the move, not taking into account all of those who left the then Yugoslavia. Why? Because it is evident that if it was only 2 million in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then if you look at the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, then the overall number of people who were on the move is much bigger, people who moved from their places of residence. That is how these two paragraphs can be interpreted. Within the Yugoslav republics, 2 million people moved, and let's add to that something that is not written here: There are people who left the area altogether and therefore the figure exceeds 2 million, because only Bosnia-Herzegovina had these 2 million people who were being transferred in different ways. That would be my interpretation of the data involved, although it is not my data initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We have come to this chapter number 5, "Expelled Persons, Refugees, and Displaced Persons from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Serbia and Montenegro." Professor, you are already used to the first question; the source of information for what you state in this chapter?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is the area of another state now, that is to say, the then State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, underneath every table the primary source is referred to, that is to say, the census of refugees and other war-affected persons in the FR Yugoslavia. This was compiled in 1996 by the UNHCR, that is referred to here, and the commissariat of the Republic of Serbia. And I took this over from the aforementioned book as a secondary source of information. So the methodology is the same as in the previous case of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, those were the only relevant institutions that used a certain methodology to register refugees and other war-affected persons, and we used those data as the most relevant at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, what about that area? Did members of all the ethnic groups of Bosnia-Herzegovina move into that area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from these tables that, yes, that was indeed the case; however, the numbers involved were different. You see here, inside these tables, that it was Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Montenegrins, Yugoslavs, others, as they had declared themselves at the time. So members of all three ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavs and others who declared themselves that way in the last census in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and the other Yugoslav republics at the time. So, yes, and it is quite evident from these statistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the results of this census that you referred to, these displaced persons and refugees, again you worked on this table, if I'm not mistaken, that is, Annex B of your paper. In the Serbian version it starts on page 156. In English, if I'm not mistaken, it is 157. So could you please find it, and perhaps we can hear your comments on what you had written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please look at the next page both in English and in Serbian. It starts with Banja Luka. The next page, please. Again we have the subheading, so we need the next page with the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, could you please help us with this now. Can you help us find our way here. Let us take Banja Luka, and perhaps Bijeljina as well, as examples. As we see from the heading, this information pertains to municipalities of present residents and municipalities of former residents; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this means for Banja Luka, this number up here that says "total" in bold? 132.298, can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that number mean?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel it is necessary to explain these tables because they are not all that simple. The municipalities of present residents are referred to in bold in the middle of the page. For example, Banja Luka, where certain persons moved in. Whereas municipalities of former residents are referred to underneath this number individually of 22.000 et cetera. A total of 132.298 is a figure that pertains to all of Republika Srpska, but that is the number of households that had moved, not of inhabitants. As for individual inhabitants, the number is about 450.000. So then these households are further differentiated within individual municipalities from which these people had moved. We are going to use the example of the municipality of Banja Luka. Banja Luka is the municipality where, according to the census of 1996, 22.582 households moved in from other municipalities. I repeat, this is the number of households, not inhabitants. Multiply it by an average of four and then you're going to get the actual number of individual inhabitants. Then what follows are municipalities from which people moved into Banja Luka. You have an entire spectrum here, from Bileca all the way to Slavonia, that is to say, the area of Croatia and so on. For example, Bileca 2 means two households from Bileca moved to Banja Luka. For example, Bugojno, 431. It is quite evident from these figures that the population moved into these municipalities from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina or from neighbouring Croatia where there were war processes in the previous period as well. Then we see the municipality of Bijeljina and so on and so forth. So could this information please be reliably interpreted, if I have explained this properly. So this is a description of households, not actual individuals who were displaced persons. According to the Census of Displaced Persons and Refugees in Republika Srpska in 1996, that involved a figure of over one-third of its total population at the time. Counsel, if I was clear enough, that is the explanation I have to provide. If it is not clear, I stand ready to provide further explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, could you just explain the reason why you chose to focus on the number of households rather than taking the number of physical persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. The reason is that when a census of refugees and displaced persons was conducted, those who were provided with temporary accommodation in these municipalities, accommodation was provided for households as units rather than for individual inhabitants regardless of whether they were from one in the same household or family, or just individuals. Of course, I could have added alongside this data the data that pertains to the individual number of refugees and displaced persons, but the point here was to show how households were moved away because they are wholes, they were socio-economic wholes, and were in this period temporarily accommodated in some other areas outside of their earlier places of residence. This was the reason why I decided to present the data in this manner. But the data on the number of individually displaced persons is available and it can be presented easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, this table -- I'm sorry, one of the Judges has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Professor, it's just to understand. All those places where the people came from to move into Banja Luka, they are more or less alphabetically ordered, right, but then at page 75 a new alphabetical order starts. Could you explain that? It's from Bileca to Zivinice, if I pronounce that well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- and then the alphabet starts again, from Beli Manastir to Zadar. I mean, what's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The alphabetical order was not taken into account here because, as you can see, Sanski Most precedes Ilijas, and in alphabet I is always before S, so this was not a priority when listing it, though it could be a rule that alphabetical order should be applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What did you apply then? Or is it just random?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, one could not say literally random because that would mean that data was imaginary, but from the sources of information and secondary sources which are listed, they are listed in this way, without a rule having to do with alphabetical order or any other principles. Let me call it arbitrary, but correct, citing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, your table is inverted in part and begins with Banja Luka once again but now municipalities of former residents are first. I will just mention the page where it begins: It's 1D06-2346.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, before leaving this one, can I ask one more question. Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- there are 287 households, municipality of present residence Banja Luka and municipality of former residence Banja Luka. Does that mean that they moved within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just looking for the subheadings to see why this is repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The first line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forty-six; is that what you have in mind? Page number 46?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Seventy-four, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, it's on the first page you dealt with. Judge Delvoie means --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zero six; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. And in the third column Judge Delvoie pointed your attention to Banja Luka where it says 287.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. These were movements within the borders of the municipality or the town of Banja Luka. Within it. So from one unidentified settlement, they would move to a different settlement which is also part of Banja Luka. That also happened as part of the migration, so it shouldn't be confusing or bring into doubt the exact data provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, let me just see whether we have the second part of the table on the screen. It begins with Banja Luka once again.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 46.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1D06-2346. And we see a change here, the municipality of former residences -- first, have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next, which is listed as the municipality of present residence. Can you please explain what this data mean.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professionally speaking, it means inversion. Okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please explain in more detail.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the area of Banja Luka -- MR. Di FAZIO: Page 111, if Your Honours please, you'll find it in English. 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. I did not say that and it was my omission, but we have the correct page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I think you may continue now.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the so-called inverted process which we call a counter-tendency. Households are moving in the opposite direction for certain reasons, as mentioned here, though I would keep reservation about certain information because I took it over from somewhere else. I'm not sure if it's well represented in the tables. But essentially I think it's the inverted process of population leaving or moving in, and the assumption is that they are from other ethnic groups. But the ethnicity is not mentioned here but I'm persuaded that this is what that's all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Professor, at the bottom of this table and the previous one, as I think Judge Delvoie noticed, one can see that there are many municipalities from the territory of the Republic of Croatia as municipalities of former residence, and these persons are then placed in the municipalities of present residence in Republika Srpska. Can you please explain this process for us.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known that there was forced migration in the territory of Republic of Croatia, even earlier than before this began in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, because there was armed conflict there as well. The majority of the Serbian population that inhabited certain areas of Croatia, and they are listed here, areas such as Slavonia or Slavonska Pozega or Podravska Slatina, and some maritime towns close to the Lika region in Croatia, or even from Slovenia where there were some conflicts even earlier, there was a wave of refugees coming from there and most of them were Serbs moving into the more ethnically homogenised areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is evident from the data. And let me add that presently there are tens of thousands of refugees who have moved into Bosnia-Herzegovina from Croatia and whose status has not been fully resolved yet, even though according to the international convention of 1951 they are under international protection, but there are still tens of thousands of such people living in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The data has been included according to the census from 1996, but the numbers have changed since then, both in terms of the spatial division of the population and in terms of the numbers of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Professor, are there any data or assessments of the number of people who, so to speak, have passed through the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and only remained in certain places temporarily and then moved on, for example, in the direction of Serbia or Sandzak and so on? Is such data available, or such estimates?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why after the war a census was conducted, in order to determine the number of refugees and displaced persons. And this was done on several occasions because the status of these people kept changing as well as their spatial distribution in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have to object to any moving into this subject of people who have moved through the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There's not one jot of evidence in this report detailing statistics or the sources of such statistics or the methods of analysis of such statistics of people transiting through Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nothing. And now we are going into it and we're going to now, no doubt, get lots of pronouncements on statistics and estimates and so on, but it's not been covered in the report. And furthermore, it's just simply not relevant to any of the issues in trial. But most of all, it just hasn't been covered in the report. It's a whole new area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain, Your Honours. I partly agree with my learned friend, the Prosecutor, but the question has a foundation, namely the testimony of an expert witness is evidence. Why am I asking him this? The Prosecutor prejudges my question and it is this: Whether the temporary residence of these persons in an area affected the movements of the local population. This is what I wanted to ask. So the witness can answer both of my questions at one and the same time. MR. Di FAZIO: The problem is -- the problem is we've got to have some evidence or some statistics on temporary residence. When was this temporary residence, where was the temporary residence, what's the source of the statistics for the temporary residence, is -- are those -- is that material in these reports? It's, I'm afraid, irrelevant and it's a bit glib to say that just because the witness is an expert he can give us those statistics.
