utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which, Mr. Cvijetic, the basis, the fundamental point of the objection is that the witness is wandering outside of his report. So on what basis is the Chamber being invited to receive this new evidence which, as Mr. Di Fazio also says, has no -- being outside the report, there's no foundation for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not have the intention to elaborate this issue in detail. The essence is in just one question. We do not have to deal with data, even though the expert witness began to talk about census and lists of such persons. But let us not allow him to present this data because he did not include that in the report. Let me just phrase the question like this:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these persons by their temporary residence change the ethnic composition of certain places in which they resided for a time and did this have an impact on the general movements of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I think I will stick to the numbers listed from the census from which one can see that the movements of the population from the territory of Croatia to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mostly those that are predominantly populated by Serbs, did affect temporarily the change of the ethnic makeup of the population, because the majority of these refugees and displaced persons went in the direction of the then Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the so-called third countries, which was later on confirmed by data from the census conducted in 2000. The number was much reduced. I already said that the number was several tens of thousands of refugees who left the territory of Croatia and then moved into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina but they mostly moved on to the territory covered by Republika Srpska. That is the essence of the data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move to the last subject with which I will finish the examination of the witness today, which I will leave for after the break, just answer a couple of questions, Professor, that have to do with the issue of the return of population from these categories. Are there any serious studies available at the moment that deal with this subject, and is there any data available about the return of these persons to the areas from which they moved out? Who is doing this sort of research, is there any data available, and where can the data be found? Just briefly so that we can finish off this subject.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to avoid any confusion, I did not elaborate this data in my report but I am willing to state them precisely and to answer your question. Of course, certain institutions at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its entities have continuously kept records, as I think they may most precisely be called, about these persons. It is obvious that very often we do not conduct a census because a census is a more comprehensive phenomenon. At this moment I can say that in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina we have a much more favourable picture in terms of return of refugees and displaced persons who have returned to the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 527.000 persons still remain outside the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the category of refugees who enjoy international protection according to the convention from 1951 and the protocol from 1967. On the other hand, there is another 450.000 displaced persons, so there within the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is close to 1 million people. That means that earlier more than 1 million people returned either from outside the borders or from -- or within Bosnia-Herzegovina to their former places of residence. This is official information from UNHCR, the Ministry for Human Rights of Refugees of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the entities' statistical bureaus or institutions such as the ministries for refugees and displaced persons. And I have the data before me and if necessary we can mention exact numbers, though I should emphasise that the data relates to 2006 as the last year listed. What I know from my own research, the data is still subject to change and the situation is even more favourable now, as the number of refugees and displaced persons has been further reduced. I can elaborate that on the example of both entities if need be. All in all, the process is on-going, and I'm due to emphasise that in the legal sense each refugee or displaced person in the territory of Republika Srpska is now able to access their property. This has been completed and now it is up to each person to choose his or her residence, to choose where he or she would live. As for myself, even though I have managed to recover my property, I remained residing in another place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have told you which municipalities are mentioned in the indictment. Do you have the same data for those municipalities, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Banja Luka, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that piece of paper but I can use a map. Prijedor, territorially speaking, belongs to Republika Srpska. The return of the population to that municipality has occurred to a large degree. That goes especially for Kozarac, where before the war Muslims were dominant population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you gave me the paper in question during the preparation for the testimony, and I can maybe give it to you, through the usher, if you can use it.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could use it. MR. Di FAZIO: I don't think I've seen this paper. And if Your Honours please, perhaps I should object to this evidence. It's -- I don't follow the relevance of showing returns to these particular municipalities. It may be that people have returned to Prijedor or Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I suggest, Mr. Di Fazio, that before you formulate your objection, you look at the piece of paper? MR. Di FAZIO: Yes. Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That's a good suggestion. I'll adopt it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me first whether this is the document that you have in mind? Maybe I made a mistake. If it isn't, maybe you could give us the numbers based on your memory.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? MR. Di FAZIO: Well, I've seen the paper. I think I maintain my objection. First of all, it's in B/C/S. Although doing the best that I can, it doesn't seem to include all the indictment municipalities as is suggested. And secondly, it seems to span the period 1991 to 2007, so I don't know if the witness can give times of when people returned. But even if he were able to give times to when people returned, I assume he's talking about later periods of time post-war; that's what I gather from the evidence. What's the relevance of it? And that's the general objection. We could wrap up this topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to withdraw the paper, and my question is going to be of a principle character. Maybe the witness should answer the way that he began. I would like him to tell us where this process was most pronounced among the municipalities listed in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not have to give us any data; you can just speak globally.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. For me, the relevance of these data is as follows: They show the total demographic capacities of those municipalities from 1991 to 2007. That is the period covered by official estimates and data. The essence of the message contained within the data is that those human capacities are declining regardless of the fact that the war is now finished. The population continues to emigrate from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is one message. The other message speaks about the change of the ethnic structure of the current inhabitants in those municipalities. The data start with 1991, and for 2007 the boxes are empty because we do not have official data for those local communes. And I have based my estimates on official estimates here. Those estimates come from official statistical institutions. As far as the intensive return, the return is most intensive precisely in large population centres such as Prijedor, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Banja Luka. So these are the largest population centres in the territory of Republika Srpska. If you permit me to say, around 200.000 returnees came to the territory of Republika Srpska between the end of the war and today. We cannot establish exactly who returned when; however, we know that this comprises around 20 per cent of the total population of Republika Srpska. At the same time, in the Federation the same process is somewhat slower. There, the Bosniak and Muslim population comprises 95 per cent of the total population. There are only up to 4 per cent Serbs. While according to 1991 census, there was 17.6 per cent of Serbs. I have already explained that yesterday and I can elaborate it today if necessary. So we see that those movement are very complex, and I'm continuously trying to say that the ethnic homogenisation is still going on in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is one of my key findings, and this process is still on-going. All the data mentioned confirm this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before we go for a break, let me ask my last question before the break. We've just seen the tables pertaining to Banja Luka, Bijeljina, et cetera containing the data about the number of households, persons who chose Bijeljina in Republika Srpska as their permanent residence. Now, those data pertain to 1996; could you tell me whether the situation in 1996 is identical to the situation today and what kind of process are we facing here in terms of return of the population and moving back?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not identical in terms of the change of status of displaced persons. At the time, those people had a status of displaced person. In the meantime, many of them have resolved the issue of their permanent residence. The fact that testifies to this is also that Banja Luka and Bijeljina have more inhabitants than they had in 1991. All other municipalities, both in the Federation and Republika Srpska, have less inhabitants. Those are the demographic losses that we mentioned earlier. However, many persons lost the status of displaced person, and that's why the number went down. So they solved their situations by various means and now they reside outside the places of the permanent residence in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know one thing specifically, and that is whether the number of people arriving is growing compared to 1996, is it still growing today? This ethnic homogenisation that you mentioned, is it still on the increase and whether those people are still on the move? Are Serbs arriving to Banja Luka and Bijeljina even today?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have proofs of that, the data collected by the federal statistical agency of the BiH as well as the statistical agency of Republika Srpska. They published yearly the data on internal migration, and you can clearly see from that the fact that the population is moving still today. And only Republika Srpska has a positive migration count. So in order to conclude: The process of ethnic territorial homogenisation within Bosnia-Herzegovina is still going on, and the homogenisation of ethnic territories is still going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one more topic for this witness. I think that I'm going to conclude my examination-in-chief today, and I would ask maybe five minutes more for the break so that we can have a proper rest and then we can finish the examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would reconvene at 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, we are going to conclude this examination-in-chief with the last topic. This is the topic that we requested you to comment on. We requested you to comment the expert report compiled by the team of experts led by Ewa Tabeau as well as others. Your comments begin at paragraph 109, so you should turn to the relevant page now. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to retell what you wrote in the report. During the examination-in-chief -- MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless I've missed -- I just think it's a mistake: I think the commentary actually begins at -- towards the end of the report. It's not paragraph 109. I think it's ... sorry, just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 199. 199. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During my examination-in-chief, you referred several times to this part of the report and you mentioned some of your criticisms. However, here in this part of the report you present your comments on the report submitted by the Prosecution expert. Could you now recapitulate and summarise for the Trial Chamber your basic criticisms of the study compiled by Ms. Tabeau, methodologically speaking. And, of course, you do not need to repeat things that are already in the report, but just give us a brief overview. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, we should know which of the three reports we're dealing with here or, if not, whether the comments apply equally to all three and whether the comments are intended to apply equally to all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all three reports were admitted into evidence in this case. In his introduction, the expert refers to all three reports, and my question was of a general nature. I am referring to the methodology of work, so the comments should apply to all three experts, but I think that our expert will be in a position to explain this in a better way than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, have you heard?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, but I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So these are my comments or, to put it more precisely, a critical commentary on the reports that have been submitted in a number of cases by Ms. Tabeau and other associates which are based on certain facts which, if you permit me, I intend to interpret here as well as present some general conclusions. I think that it is very important to show on specific examples how some conclusions were erroneous and how some data were miscalculated. But I think that it will be most useful if I start from general conclusions and then move on to specific questions. The methodological approach adopted in the report of Ms. Tabeau and associates is mainly based on statistical and mathematical methods, that is, the law of numbers. This is insufficient for a research of such complexity. After all, such a research is based on calculations by way of numbers. There is a maxime in the statistical science saying that the number will tell you only as much as the person who plays with it want you to know. What is missing from these reports are different methodological approaches. First of all, the reports lack a more intensive empirical research. It is understandable to a certain degree because the authors of the reports could not go into the field at the relevant time. And to be quite honest, this is the advantage of my report because I was there in the relevant area while certain acts were occurring, acts that I have attempted to include in my report by way of a professional and scientific elaboration. So besides the fact that this report does not have a proper methodological approach, it is quite clear that the work is not based on proper sources of data. There are objective and subjective reasons for that. The only source of data that cannot be disputed is the population census of 1991, but I have to emphasise in relation to that one thing: We in Bosnia and Herzegovina never had data that were officially published and comprehensively processed. I mean, here, the data pertaining to the 1991 census. They were published only by the Federal Statistics Bureau, and before that only the ethnic composition and some other data were published by the Croatian State Statistical Institute in Zagreb. All this means, that the calculation of some important parameters in this report was based on estimates, and these estimates are very flexible. These estimates are based on an unreliable database. There are various registers of institutions whose main line of business is not the collection of demographical data. They compile their registers for their own use. I noticed several similar sources. Even the authors of the reports themselves say for some of the sources that they are unreliable and that they are based on some estimates that do not reflect the reality. So these are some of the comments. Furthermore, there is the question of the consistency of reports on some of the victims, such as ethnic group. And another very important question, status of soldier or civilian. I was not able to find in the reports the methodology which would start from the general situation at the beginning of the war and then the subdivision into civilians and soldiers, and yet the reports speak about the civilian and military casualties. It is very difficult to accept these data as relevant if you do not know the general overview of a phenomenon in question. Why am I saying that? The military civilian status has often been manipulated for some subjective reasons. For instance, people were able to gain certain advantages because they were registered as soldiers. Or for instance, a family might gain some advantage if they register a victim as a soldier although such a victim was not actually a soldier. So the authors had to be more precise about who belonged to the military. It was only the officers, the people at the front line, and the people who are currently on furlough or hospitalised. Everybody else is, according to international standards, civilians. So such a classification is something that I cannot find in the reports, because it is the only thing that would enable me to estimate the accuracy of the data. Further on, you can see that the reports contain some databases that are more complete and some that are less complete. In cases where we have more complete databases, we can obtain a more reliable result. As I have already said, the reliability of the sources of data is something that is not really very reliable for these reports. If you look at the registers pertaining to the military or municipalities or other civilian institutions, you will see that these are the registers that do not have the appropriate statistical forms. And numbers are very easy things to manipulate. Further on, I was not able to conclude that the reports used standardised documents in order to prove, by use of the standardised document, how data on number of casualties were collected or how data on number of expelled persons were collected. I have already mentioned standardised data. It is my assessment that there are no such standardised data in these documents, and that can lead to a deformed picture about a certain fact. So in my studies I used exclusively standardised documents, uniformed forms issued by certain institutions, containing certain questions that pertain to each and every individual. What else is important here? Although the authors used various but quite unreliable sources of data, they could have used some other documents for such a study, especially bearing in mind that the creation of those reports begin some five years after the war. As far as I was able to ascertain, Ms. Tabeau has been engaged in this research since 2000. So it was possible to use other sources of data. Why am I saying this? I will quote Ms. Tabeau herself, which I already did. In giving a similar professional opinion about a similar research by the documentation centre in Sarajevo, she says, and I quote: "That the study should not contain a small number of the sources of data, that the sources have to be different in order to avoid biased statistics, and in order to create a historical and accurate picture." And I can maybe add one more thing: We don't know whether they managed to eliminate duplicates. Because there were manipulations, a certain person could have been registered both as a soldier and a civilian for purely subjective reasons such as gaining certain material advantages. I call that a less competent record-keeping, and that is what was used in this paper. Extensive sources were used, as they're called, as well as the database of deceased persons in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995. I claim that at that point in time such data was not kept in order either in the Federation or in Republika Srpska. Why am I saying that? If we look at the statistical yearbooks in Bosnia-Herzegovina then if we look at the database, you do not have this information. There are hyphens there as regards the number of deceased persons as a result of war operations directly or indirectly. That database is only regulated from 1996 onwards, and that is how we use the data involved in our own scientific research. The ICRC list of missing persons was used, as it is referred to. That is a question that not very much light has been shed on in Bosnia-Herzegovina because there are still quite a few persons who are considered to be missing and whose fate is still unknown. Then exhumed and unidentified persons; records of such persons are not properly kept in Bosnia-Herzegovina to this day, although there is a joint institute that deals with the matter. There are quite a few questions that are still unresolved. Then there are certain lists that were compiled by NGOs, rather unreliable lists because in that period of time these organisations did not have the proper professional and other capacities to provide reliable data. Every one of the mentioned sources in these reports, as an answer is sought to specific questions, has to provide firm, reliable data, and I think that that is one of the shortcomings here. As concerns the number of victims in war - this is something I particularly wish to highlight - to this day there is not a single source in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, not a single institution in Bosnia-Herzegovina that came to a final figure. I think that in the foreseeable future that will remain difficult. However, let us state objectively the research of Ms. Tabeau and her co-workers and the research of the Information Documentation Centre in Sarajevo dealt with this subject matter in the most comprehensive manner. As you know, the number of -- the total number of victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was published in the book "War in Figures," it is 104.732. And then there is the figure of 98.000, as far as children are concerned. I don't think that this can be the final figure. I don't know what the figure may be. I know it is not less. I know that it may only be more. However, this refutes the exaggerated figures of 200- or 300.000 deceased persons in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, within all of these figures that were presented there is quite a bit of concrete evidence as to the structure of victims according to ethnic affiliation is wrong or insufficient [as interpreted]. I specifically point that out in papers for the Information and Documentation Centre. I think that that can be proven in this paper as well. So let us conclude these general remarks. Any paper that deals with this subject, if proper scientific methods are used, valid sources of information, and so on, is very useful. But at this point in time we have not come to final or exact figures yet. I can say that for my own papers too, although I did not deal with the total number of victims because I did not have the individual capacity to do so. But there is another mosaic that I put together of demographic changes in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period from 1992 to 1995, and that may be complementary to these reports. Along with all these improvements, in the foreseeable future perhaps we may come it a more objective and more realistic report that pertains to the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to conclude on this note, but I would like to ask that I later be allowed to give some concrete examples to show how some things were wrongly calculated and done in this report that I am providing a critical review of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'm giving you that chance right away. Choose one or two examples but not too many because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you allow me, there's some clarification I would like to ask the witness. Professor, you said the total number of -- in the transcript: "... the total number of victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was published in the book 'War in Figures,' it is 104.732." And then the transcript says: "And then there is the figure of 98.000, as far as children are concerned." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know what the interpretation was, but it is IDC research. Those are their results. And IDC is headed by Mirsad Tokaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when it is pronounced in our language, that particular abbreviation "IDC," it sounds like the word for "children" phonetically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the figure for 98.000 is the IDC figure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, before you continue, Mr. Cvijetic. Professor, taking you back to the earlier part of your explication, why -- if I understood you correctly, you considered your report to have an advantage over the reports on which you adversely commented, the fact that you were able to make certain observations in the field which the authors of those reports were not able to. Could you explain why in your view this is considered an advantage? And couldn't the contrary be also argued that the -- that your own observations in the field would have somehow muddied the water, as it were, in terms of the objectivity of the data with which you were dealing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I did not say that my paper was better. Perhaps you misunderstood what I said. I said that it was indispensable as a complementary paper to all such papers. From different sources and different papers, we get a clearer and more objective picture. This is to say that I did not underestimate this comprehensive research that was carried out, but I said quite specifically that there are quite a few shortcomings there. If all papers of this nature are taken into account when such serious extensive research is being carried out, then one gets a more objective picture of all the developments involved. I did not have the sufficient capacity and logistics. I didn't have anything that would match what these researchers had, but I think it would be very useful, where I can prove this by way of facts, I refute some of the things stated by these authors. That is what I'm trying to do now, and that is what I would like to tell you now so that you would see that this is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, before you give some examples -- perhaps it would be a good idea actually if you would give your examples first, and then I'm going to put these questions to you that are based on Judge Hall's question, and I meant to leave that for the end anyway. So if you have such examples, could you please refer to them now so that I could complete my examination by putting a question that is identical to the question phrased by Judge Hall.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I will start with paragraph 232, where I am referring to the estimated data of the population in 1991 older than those born in 1980. I claim that this is unrealistic and that that can be proven easily. In Ms. Tabeau's report, there are data for persons before -- born before 1980 and they are based on estimates, statistical and mathematical estimates. I illustrated this in paragraph 233, taking, as an example, the municipality of Bijeljina, where Ms. Tabeau's report said that as for Bijeljina the total population including all ethnicities in 1991 born before 1980 was 81.650. That is data that she provides. May I remind you that according to the 1991 census for Bijeljina, the total population of Bijeljina was 96.988 and that can be seen in paragraph 230. Now, where is the error? According to this, it turns out that in the area of the municipality of Bijeljina, 84.18 per cent of the population was born in 1980 and older than that. Those were persons who were of age and who had the right to vote, according to Ms. Tabeau's report. I claim that that is incorrect. Such an unfavourable index of the age of the population of the Bijeljina municipality was not there in 1991, and this index is the relationship between the old and the young population. Here we are talking about the young population, persons born after 1980. Why am I saying that? Why do you claim that? I would like to direct you to paragraph 253. What I provide here, on the basis of the 1991 census, is the age structure of the population of the municipality of Bijeljina according to age contingents. It is evident that the share of the young population considerably exceeds the mentioned 16 per cent that Ms. Tabeau refers to. For all municipalities, including Bijeljina, that share ranges between 23 to 30 per cent. It is impossible that in only seven or eight years the population of Bijeljina aged, under quotation marks, so quickly and that we got this oversized number of adults who are of age, that is to say, those who were born before 1980. That is what I showed here in a few paragraphs. Analogous to that would be conclusions for other municipalities that are referred to. Another important thing to say is that the highest share in the young population up until the age of 18 was registered among the Muslim population because they had a considerably higher natural birth-rate as compared to the Serb and Croatian populations - I even referred to that for BH as a whole - 14 per cent; Croats, 8 per cent; and Serbs, 7 per cent. That unequivocally leads us to the conclusion that the Muslim population has a bigger share among the younger population rather than those born before 1980. So may I say that this number of persons born in Bijeljina before 1980 is an overexaggerated one and then it sheds a different light on Ms. Tabeau's report. That is the first example that I wish to provide that involves erroneous calculation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've mentioned the rest in your paper. Professor, I would now like to go back to the context of Judge Hall's question, and I want to place your paper within that context. I wish to ask you the following: In a way, you chose your view of your paper on your own. If you were to observe your own paper with the same critical eyes, how would you assess it and how would you view it in terms of its relevance for this Trial Chamber as compared to Ms. Ewa Tabeau's paper? This is my specific question. MR. Di FAZIO: That's a question for Your Honours, not for the witness, for Mr. Cvijetic, or myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wish to put a specific question now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your paper a negation of Ms. Ewa Tabeau's paper or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I try to be clear and yet objective. All such papers are useful. However, even the best of papers have to be subjected to a critical review. That is a rule in science. That's way it is. They're all useful, but none of them can be considered to be final in terms of painting a picture of certain developments. Let me be perfectly honest and say that that is how I view my very own paper as well. It has not given an answer to many questions, but it did deal with some questions in a more comprehensive way than these other papers did. My advantage was the fact that I was a direct participant in all these events and that I have a better knowledge of the area involved and therefore it was easier for me in that way to get to some relevant results, though I appreciate what was presented in Ms. Tabeau's extensive research. However, I repeat, that is only statistics and mathematics. From a distance, you cannot fully be familiar with a certain area and certain developments only through mathematics and statistics, especially if these developments do not always follow a certain logic. Statisticians and mathematicians cannot deal with it in that way only, and I showed you an example that indicates that we cannot take an average when we look at, say, the population before -- born before 1980. Every local territory, every local region, has specific characteristics of its own, as opposed to this average that we call Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now I'm going to say that there is something that statistics says, by way of a joke, in a way that statistics itself is the greatest deception of all. Or, rather, average in statistics is the greatest deception of all. That is to say that averages have to be well-founded, because I tried to show that every territorial unit including the very smallest one have very specific characteristics of their own and those who know them best can give the most objective picture, of course if they also applied well-known scientific methods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, and can you admit that Ms. Ewa Tabeau objectively had problems and was unable to achieve even better results? Would you have met with the same problems if you had taken the same path as she did?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I never discussed the subjectivity of Ms. Ewa Tabeau but, rather, objective problems and objective lack of knowledge of the area or lack of possibility to collect relevant data which would enable her to reach the results that she was striving for. I have begun to study her very extensive book "The War in Figures," which treats the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No one has analysed it -- no one has provided this up until this time, but you cannot take it for granted. Beginning with the smallest territorial units, it can be refuted. But as a conclusion, it doesn't mean that I denigrate her work or believe it to be irrelevant. It simply needs more works that would be added to it so that we would have a more complete picture of the historical events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This has to be placed in a historical context and conclusions have to be based on facts. As I said earlier, there are no compromises in science. Bosnia-Herzegovina is full of compromises, but in politics, not in science, however. We are struggling to reach the truth regardless of which ethnicity we are of. I believe that I made a certain contribution for a more comprehensive study of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Together with other works, mine should add additional data to the study. Unfortunately there are few of such works, but that imposes on us an obligation to strive to reach a more objective picture with exact facts. When we will be able to do so, it is difficult to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On several occasions you said for your work that you wanted to produce a complementary study. Do you mean that it should have been complementary of Ms. Ewa Tabeau's study, in the context of your last answer, that both works taken together should be worth more than each of them individually?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this research and this process, the answer is yes. I would wish my report to be complementary to the other studies. And outside the context, I still believe that it would be complementary to some other studies. I do not claim that I'm the only one who would be able to answer all questions in this field of study; that would go way beyond my abilities. But after a few years of research, I have presented something that can be very useful in the series of these works, and it's based on scientific research. There are other researches which are not based on scientific principles and that are not relevant for such a significant project.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Professor, you have completed your report by a chapter which is entitled "General Conclusions on the Migratory Movements for Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Period Between 1992 and 1995." There are no paragraphs there. Let me just say that the page is 1D06-2219. 1D06-2219. Professor, it is page 71 in the pages you have.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not ask you to read it out. Please finish your testimony or at least the examination-in-chief by a general conclusion that the Trial Chamber could draw from your report. What is the substance of your claims as presented in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance of my claims, and I hope the evidence presented in the report, especially with a view to the period of 1992 to 1995, is ethnic territorial homogenisation and a simplification of the ethnic mosaic in some areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is one thing. Another conclusion that I wanted to point out in the conclusions, which follow as the summary of what you have presented throughout the report, is that not one report from this field can be focussed on just year of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina because then unequivocally the picture you would get would be distorted. I especially emphasise the year 1992 because it presents a distorted picture of the entire situation during the war, because the war was a process. It was not a short-lived phenomenon. Therefore it is necessary to take into account the whole period, and this is why my report is focused on the whole period between 1992 and 1995. I wanted to point out that all the events that took place between 1992 and 1995 caused major demographic changes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, just like any other war. And in terms of the total number of population of the composition in terms of age, sex, and ethnicity, the reduced capacities, by which I mean the fertility, also the redistribution of the population and also its eugenic or qualitative characteristics, if you allow me, that was not a subject of the report because I had not done my work in connection with that. But I can just briefly say what the demographic losses in Bosnia-Herzegovina have been during the war and after it by using information from other institutions and also what I collected during my own research. If we begin by saying that, conditionally speaking, the number of victims is 104.732, according to the information of Ewa Tabeau who studied this in more detail, then the greatest losses were those caused by the immigration -- emigration of population; I mean the demographic losses, because 527.000 people are outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Fertility has been reduced due to the war, and on that basis Bosnia-Herzegovina has lost several tens of thousands of people. When I talk about demographic losses, just to be clear, I start from a premise what would have happened had there been no war. There would have been 800.000 inhabitants more in Bosnia-Herzegovina if the war had not taken place, if no one had been killed, if no people had emigrated, and if the birth-rate had not been reduced due to the war. Of course there are other processes which contributed to that which are obvious in Europe and in the world which is the more pronounced aging of the population and the reduced fertility of the population. All these problems burdened demographic development of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, thank you. Your Honours, I have finished examination-in-chief of Professor Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do you confirm your earlier position that you have no questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to begin your cross-examination? MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's quarter past. Would you permit me to simply start on one discrete topic. I say that because I had prepared my cross-examination on the basis of the reports and altered it to a certain extent on the basis of yesterday's evidence, but the evidence that's come in today may have the result of shortening my cross-examination and I hope to do that and ensure that I'm completely finished tomorrow. That's my aim. But I need to rearrange it in order to achieve that. So I would like to be given that opportunity to do that. I do have one short, discrete topic that I could start on now, if you prefer me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you. Cross-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, Professor Pasalic, about your past studies. I think you completed a teacher's college course in Travnik in 1970 and then you went to the Academy for - never sure how to pronounce this - Pedagogy in Slavonski Brod in 1973; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a teacher's college, isn't it, it's a place where teachers are taught how to teach?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then you went to the mathematics faculty in Novi Sad and there you obtained a bachelor of arts degree in geography; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematic, not just mathematics, which has a separate department for geography. And geography is a science about space. So once you get your degree, you get a degree in geography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Sorry, geography. And that was in 1979, that was your first academic qualification, a bachelor's; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was another diploma which I got from the Academy for Pedagogy, and that is a higher-education institution. Pedagogical academy is another institution of higher education where you get a diploma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. You started your post-graduate work in 1979 with a master's degree in Belgrade and you defended that degree, which I take to mean you obtained it, in 1983, in April of 1983; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, and this was my narrow discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the title of your master's thesis?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Geographical Characteristics of the Territory of the Zavidovici Municipality and its Environment." The goal was to deal with the population and protection of the environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. So it's title was "Geographical Characteristics of the Territory of Zavidovici and its Environment"; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I could elaborate on the contents of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to elaborate any more; I just want to know the title. In your CV, you say that you got a master's in geography and demography, and that's at page 76 of your CV. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment. I cannot at this moment find what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It's page 76 in the English. It's your curriculum vitae and bibliography. It says: "The institution University of Belgrade from November 1980 to April 1983 MA in geography, demography."

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. MA in geography and the specific discipline was the graduate course which was entitled "Population," which does not bring in doubt the topic of my work. I was not obliged to study just the population, but the more complex issue of the impact of population on the environment and its protection, because it was in a way initiated by the local community to deal with such subjects which I accepted. And let me also add that I received a golden plaque as the highest merit issued by the local community for this work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. MR. Di FAZIO: Could we have 65 ter 281. 20081 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat, please. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's okay. It will come up on the screen. Don't worry. I want to put -- just lead you to an extract in your book. It's at page 2 of the English, and it has your photo on the top left-hand corner. So I think it's probably the second page in the book. It's page 2 of the English, which is a translation of an extract from your book, the introduction, so to speak. That's it. There it says -- there it says in the first part of the book dealing with you and your background that you got your master's degree at the Faculty of Natural Sciences in Belgrade in 1983 in the field of tourism and protection of the environment. Is that what your master's was about, tourism and protection of the environment, as stated in your own book?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it says in the book. It was an error made by the editor and the editorial board. It is imprecise, even though during studying population there was some interaction with the study of tourism. But this is a secondary source which is not relevant for my CV and bibliography.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you see, the book, if you look at the table of contents which is at page 6 of the English, and I'm afraid I don't know what it is in the B/C/S, but it's about 3 or 4 pages on, page 6, you see that the book is all about population demographics, migrations, demographic reality of the Serbian people. The entire book is all about demographics, so you would have paid attention, wouldn't you, to accurately portraying your qualifications in this book which is all about demographics? It would have been important to you to highlight your career -- sorry, your academic qualifications in demographics in this book, but yet it says that you've got a master's degree in the field of tourism and protection of the environment. Surprising, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diplomas are relevant. They are the academic qualifications. Obviously the editorial board did not have at hand my diplomas. The very fact that the book is about the demographics testifies to the direction of my scientific interest. However, besides the demography as my primary interest, I've already testified yesterday that I'm also qualified as a social geographer. And within the field of study of social geography is also the field of tourism, which is a discipline that falls within the purview of that field. I agree it's a little bit contradictory, and, yes, I agree that it should have been mentioned in a more precise way in order to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if -- it seems that your interest in tourism -- nothing wrong with that, of course, but your interest in tourism continued, because if you look at your published scholarly papers at page 79 of your report, page 79 of your report, it's all part of this section dealing with your curriculum vitae and publications, and the section headed "Published Scholarly Papers," in 1996 you produced a paper called "Tourism Potentials of the Republika Srpska." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't see what is the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting there's a problem. All I'm trying to establish is that your master's was really all about tourism and the environmental issues.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the title that I acquired after I did the graduation study, and you can also take a look at the exams that I had to pass. None of the exams related to the discipline of tourism. However, the influence of demographics and the tourism on the protection of the environment in relation to the demographic development is something that I continued to study because all these issues interact. If you take a look at the list of my published works, you will certainly see that the most dominant works are the demographic works. After that come my published articles from social geography and they are focussed on the tourism because tourism is part of social geography, according to the standards currently in force where I live, which are applied during the election process for the teachers for more narrowly specialised areas of my scientific discipline. You have to bear in mind that I have two distinct, narrow professional specialties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So in your book "Anthropogenic Reality of Serbs," when the introduction speaks about your having a master's degree in the field of tourism and protection of the environment, the failure to mention demography is just an unfortunate editorial oversight; correct? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The editor did not formulate our biographies in a most skillful way because they are not written according to the aforementioned principles. However, it wasn't really his duty to emphasise my more narrow specialty in a book like this. The contents of the book itself speaks to the fact that my primary field of study is scientific demography; you can see that in all the references quoted. If you take a comprehensive look at my bibliography, you will see that the demography is always at the first place. And you have to take into account the structure of all my articles, books, presentations, and international conferences, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not forbidden to take an interest into other disciplines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, Professor. Certainly. Let's look at some more of your qualifications. You obtained a doctorate in 1995 and you defended your thesis for that doctorate in March of 1995; right? And that was at the University of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the title?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact title of my dissertation is "Semberija: A Geographical Study with an Emphasis on the Population." After I had defended the dissertation, it acquired a status of scientific work. And then I published it as a book with a slightly changed title, and that title was "The Population of Semberija: A Demographic Study." You can find the book in my bibliography. And it is the result of my research that I have conducted during my PhD studies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in your curriculum vitae which is at page 76 of your report, it says that you have a doctorate in geography with a specialisation in demography. MR. Di FAZIO: Could we just have a look once again at 65 ter 281. Yes, thank you, the same introduction, the same page that we were looking at earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there, Professor Dr. Jovan Ilic, full professor at the Belgrade university, giving your background, says that you have a doctorate from the Faculty of Natural Sciences in Novi Sad in the field of regional geography. Now, is there any reason for his failure to account -- to include anything about your specialisation in demography, following your acquisition of this -- of your doctorate, in a book that's about demography?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there is a reason. During a short period of time, I taught regional geography because there was a need for that at the university, and since regional geography comprises everything about the population as well. However, you are elected into a more narrow scholarly specialty on the basis of your published work, on the basis of your references, so I have PhD in geographical sciences and my more narrow specialty is determined by my published work, by the references defined by the law and bylaws. And only when all the circumstances are met, only then can somebody be elected, as I was in the year 2000, to teach the subject of demography of population. So I never taught only demography. Even today I teach other subjects because we all have to fulfill a certain number of teaching hours in order to satisfy our working requirements. So every teacher or professor has primary and secondary teaching assignments. And I think simply that the professors who wrote these blurbs did not have at hand all my diplomas; they simply wrote what they wrote because they knew what I was engaged in at the moment. And that is the reason for this particular biography, although this book is of course covering the problematics of the population about every region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- sorry, but you've told us about where you were working and so on, but I'm not interested in that. I want to know how it's possible that in an introduction to your book on demography, your doctorate, a very important academic qualification, is described as being in the field of regional geography and doesn't mention anything about demographics. I don't want to know where you were working at the time. I want to know how it happened that a mistake like that occurred.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't really a mistake. Let me repeat the title of the dissertation: "Semberija," that's region. That's a more narrow area, with its own particular characteristics. So this is, of course, a study in regional geography, however it was a demographic study. That doesn't mean that other characteristics of the given area were not also researched. This was a practical study with practical applications in the particular area. Those are the most desirable studies because then you can contribute towards the -- towards finding of the solutions in a particular area. This is what it was all about. I really don't see any mistake here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agree it would have been really infinitely preferable for your -- any specialisation that you had actually obtained in your doctorate that dealt with demographics to have been included here in your introduction to your book which deals with demographics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, if I understood correctly, the Prosecution had not mounted any challenge to his expertise as a demographer, so I'm at a loss as to appreciating the usefulness of this line of questions. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes, I understand that. If Your Honours please, firstly, there's two answers to that. The first answer is the level of expertise is a matter that can be explored and properly explored, in my submission. And secondly, the research this gentleman, this witness, performed was performed between 1992 and 1995. That's when the statistics that form so-called Annex A were apparently collated and created. He had no demographic expertise at that time. He may have acquired it later. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. Di FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've heard the point. That's true, isn't it, by 1995 you really had no formal qualifications at all in demographics? Your main -- to be fair, your main field of study, your principle field of study, was geography?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my colleague is confusing the witness. In 1995 he was not performing this work. The data are from 1995 and he used those data when he was compiling this report, and I think that that is the proper question. MR. Di FAZIO: I understood that the witness had collated his data between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it? The data that you used in your expert report that forms the backbone of Annex A, that was all collected by you in between 1992 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a person can be a very good demographer without the formal title of PhD. Secondly, there is no special study of demography in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. You could acquire this qualification studying at the Faculty of Geography and partially at the Faculty of Economics. Thirdly, people with master's degree are also scholars and that's what I was doing at the time. There is no particular precondition that you would have to have a PhD in order to perform this research, so I see no problem here. I don't see that there is any problem related to whether somebody had a PhD at the time or not. This is my biography, and I cannot change it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that a good grounding in demographics would have assisted you in the methods of collating the material that you gathered in between 1992 and 1995, it would have vastly improved the methods of collation of material?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I think. I was well versed in demography. If you accept the fact that I graduated from the Faculty of Geography, you will see that one of the fundamental fields of study there is population, so that was my most relevant field of research. And the same goes for my graduate study. The most important faculties and the most important professors were the ones who led me through that subject matter. I wouldn't have had the ambition to go into demographic research on my own if I didn't have a chance to acquire such a good basis for it. You usually go and study things where you can gain the knowledge from that particular discipline, and I think that you can see that from all my references. I feel completely secure in my area of work. MR. Di FAZIO: Thank you, Professor. This would be -- I think, brings an end to this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we've reached the time which we adjourn for the day. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.
